meaning: Sakurai's name for a game's push and pull, or risk and reward: the fun of managing risks to get rewards. He calls it one part of a game's identity, not the whole.
The back-and-forth of taking risks to get rewards; used interchangeably with game essence.
Danger and opportunity as two sides of the same coin; they must be in close proximity and in the right amounts.
Game essence seen from the player side: how players manage risks to get rewards, or how they minimize losses and maximize gains, sometimes taking a bigger loss for an even bigger gain.
The Space Invaders state where cannon and invader are far apart and neither attack can land.
Space Invaders' endgame state where invaders at the bottom can't hit the cannon: ultimate risk, ultimate reward, probably a bug.
Applying heavy stress, then suddenly setting the player free; also used for charging during a risky drift and releasing for a speed burst.
The four-step loop behind most games: an obstacle, its removal, a reward that strengthens you, and the next obstacle becoming easier.
The counter-force every motion needs to feel complete, such as falling for flight or slowdowns for speed.
The thrill of barely scraping past a hazard, such as flying under a bridge.
Sakurai's method: pick what is fun, work out why (usually risk and reward), then rebuild it into an original mechanic.
Getting gains without losses inside the game's rules, such as metal slime farming; fun and memorable, but not extended to rewriting parameters.
Genre conventions taken for granted; he re-examines them at the start of each project.
The RPG exploration choice between going deeper for better spoils and getting out while you still can.
Last-moment survival options, like rotating a Tetris piece after it lands, that invite greater risk-taking.
Sources of fun other than push and pull: control feel, story, licensed fandom, simulation, building and crafting, rhythm.
Roger Caillois's four elements of play (competition, chance, imitation, vertigo); Sakurai places game essence mainly in agon.
The trade-off in licensed games, where faithfulness to the source comes first and you never get a perfect score on all fronts.
Showing how far the player has come and how far is left to the next reward.
Kirby Air Ride's aim of broadening how people play instead of encouraging one perfect method.
